transcript.text: My Panasonic NN-ST45KWBPQ is sparking inside when I heat soup, little blue flashes on the right-hand wall and a crackling noise. I stopped it. Is it safe?

You did the right thing stopping it. Don't use it again until you've found the cause. Continued arcing can damage the magnetron (the part that makes the microwaves) and can scorch the interior. The good news is that this is very often a simple, cheap fix.

## Most likely cause: the waveguide cover

On your model, the right-hand interior wall has a small rectangular panel, usually a greyish or beige sheet of mica or plastic-like board. It covers the opening where the microwaves enter the cavity. Soup is a classic culprit: splatters of fatty or salty liquid land on that cover, dry, and carbonise. Once carbonised, they conduct and spark, producing exactly the blue flashes and crackling you describe.

## What to do

1. Unplug the microwave and let it cool.
2. Rule out metal first. Check for a spoon left in the bowl, foil, a twist-tie, or a bowl with a metallic or gold rim or glaze.
3. Inspect the waveguide cover on the right wall. Look for food residue, dark spots, burn marks, or holes.
4. If it's just dirty: wipe it gently with a damp cloth and a little mild detergent, then dry it thoroughly. Don't soak it or scrub hard, since mica can flake.
5. If it's burnt, blackened, or has holes: replace it. Cleaning won't fix carbonised mica. Replacement covers are inexpensive and widely available. You can search for "Panasonic NN-ST45KW waveguide cover" or get a generic mica sheet and cut it to size using the old one as a template. It's usually held by a clip or small screw.
6. Clean the rest of the cavity, especially the ceiling and the right wall, where splatter builds up.
7. Check the interior paint. Chipped or peeling enamel exposing bare metal can also cause arcing. Small chips can be touched up with microwave-safe cavity paint, but rusted or extensive damage is a bigger issue.

## Test carefully

After cleaning or replacing the cover, put a microwave-safe cup of water inside (never run it empty) and heat for 30–60 seconds while watching.

## When to stop and get it repaired or replaced

• Sparking continues after cleaning or replacing the cover
• You notice a burning or electrical smell, smoke, loud buzzing, or humming
• It no longer heats properly (this can mean the magnetron or diode is damaged)
• The door, hinges, or seals are damaged

In those cases, have it checked by a qualified technician. Don't open the outer casing yourself, because microwaves contain a high-voltage capacitor that can hold a dangerous charge even when unplugged.

Tip for the future: cover soups and sauces with a microwave-safe lid or plate cover. That prevents the splatter that causes this in the first place.

No metal, just a plain plastic bowl of soup. The panel on the right wall is cardboard-like with a black burnt spot and greasy splatter on it, and the paint is fine with no chips. There's quite a lot of old splatter in there too, I've never really cleaned it. There was a slight burnt smell and one wisp of smoke from that spot before I switched it off. So should I replace the panel rather than clean it?

Yes, replace it. A black burnt spot means the mica has carbonised, and that spot will keep conducting and sparking however well you clean it. The wisp of smoke and burnt smell fit this: it's the splatter and the cover itself scorching. On its own that isn't a sign of anything worse, as long as it stops once the cover is replaced.

Don't use the microwave until the new cover is in. Running it without one lets grease reach the waveguide, and running it with the burnt one risks damaging the magnetron.

## Replacing the cover

1. Unplug it.
2. Remove the old cover. It's usually held by plastic clips, tabs, or one small screw. Ease it off gently, since you'll want it intact as a template.
3. Get a replacement:
• Exact part: search "Panasonic NN-ST45KW waveguide cover" or check Panasonic spares. The part number may be printed on the old cover.
• Generic mica sheet: cheap and widely sold. Trace the old cover, cut it with sharp scissors, and match any holes or notches.
4. Look behind it. Wipe away any grease you can reach on the metal around the opening with a damp cloth, and dry it. Don't push anything deep into the opening. Note any burn marks or pitting on the metal itself.
5. Fit the new cover the same way the old one came off.

## Clean the whole cavity

All that old splatter can arc too, so do this before testing:
• Wipe the ceiling, walls, and door with warm water and a little washing-up liquid, then dry everything.
• For baked-on grime, use a damp cloth with a paste of bicarbonate of soda. Avoid abrasive scourers and oven cleaner.
• Once the new cover is in, you can steam-clean in future by heating a bowl of water with lemon or vinegar for a few minutes, then wiping.

Covering soup with a microwave lid or plate from now on will stop the problem recurring.

## Test it

Heat a cup of water for 30–60 seconds and watch. No sparks, crackling, or smell means you're done.

## When to get it repaired instead

Stop using it and get it professionally repaired or replaced if:
• It still sparks with a new cover and a clean cavity
• The metal behind the cover is burnt, pitted, or holed
• Smoke or a burning smell comes from the vents or casing rather than the cavity
• It hums loudly, buzzes, or stops heating

Don't open the outer casing yourself. The capacitor inside can hold a dangerous high-voltage charge even when unplugged.
